ukmt-pink-2025-05.title: Use the diagonal
ukmt-pink-2025-05.body:
$OQ$ is a radius, so $OQ=10$ cm. The diagonals $OQ$ and $PR$ of a square have equal length, so $PR=10$ cm. In the right-angled isosceles triangle $PQR$, $PQ=QR$ and $PQ^2+QR^2=PR^2=100$, so $PQ^2=50$. The area is $\tfrac12\times PQ\times QR=\tfrac12\times50=25\ \text{cm}^2$.

**Answer: (A) $25\ \text{cm}^2$**

ukmt-pink-2025-05.title: Half the square
ukmt-pink-2025-05.body:
The area of a square is half the square of its diagonal: $\tfrac12\times10^2=50$. The triangle $PQR$ is half of the square, so its area is $25\ \text{cm}^2$.

**Answer: (A) $25\ \text{cm}^2$**

ukmt-pink-2025-07.title: Count appearances
ukmt-pink-2025-07.body:
The photos show the triples $123$, $234$, $345$, $456$, $567$, $671$. The numbers 3, 4, 5, 6 appear in three photos each, and 1, 2, 7 appear in two photos each. Each photo has exactly one gold medal, so there are 6 gold 'appearances' in total, and each of the two gold medals must therefore appear in 3 photos (since $3+3=6$, whereas a medal appearing in only 2 photos would give at most $2+3=5<6$). So 1, 2 and 7 are silver.

Photo $123$ must contain a gold medal, so 3 is gold. Photo $671$ must contain a gold medal, so 6 is gold. The sum is $3+6=9$.

**Answer: (C) 9**

ukmt-pink-2025-12.title: Build the number greedily
ukmt-pink-2025-12.body:
To make $N$ large the first digit should be as large as possible. $180=9\times20$, so the first digit is 9. The remaining five digits have product 20; the largest possible second digit is 5, leaving four digits with product 4: the largest choice is 4 first, then 1, 1, 1. So $N=954111$ with digit sum $9+5+4+1+1+1=21$.

**Answer: (E) 21**

ukmt-pink-2025-13.title: The two middle cells
ukmt-pink-2025-13.body:
Each of the two central cells (the middle row, second and third cells) touches, including diagonally, all the other cells except exactly one. A digit other than 1 or 8 has two consecutive neighbours (for example 4 is next to 3 and 5), and both would have to sit in the single cell not touching it, which is impossible. So 1 and 8 occupy the two central cells.

The shaded cell (left end of the middle row) is the one cell not touching the right central cell; the right end of the middle row is the one cell not touching the left central cell. If 1 is in the left central cell, then 2 must go in the only cell not touching it, the right end, and 7 (next to 8 in the right central cell) must go in the only cell not touching that, the shaded cell. If 8 is in the left central cell, then 7 goes at the right end and 2 goes in the shaded cell.

So the shaded cell contains 7 or 2 (and both can be completed, which is left as a check).

**Answer: (B) 2 or 7**

ukmt-pink-2025-16.title: Follow the choices
ukmt-pink-2025-16.body:
Brick 4 supports both bricks 1 and 2, so it can be removed only after both are gone. For it to be third, bricks 1 and 2 must be removed first and second, in either order, and then brick 4 must be chosen.

Start: only 1 and 2 are available. By symmetry suppose the first brick is 1 (this happens with probability 1/2 for 1 and 1/2 for 2, and the two cases are alike). Then the available bricks are 2 and 3, and brick 2 is chosen with probability $\tfrac12$. Now the available bricks are 3, 4 and 5, and brick 4 is chosen with probability $\tfrac13$. The probability is $\tfrac12\times\tfrac13=\tfrac16$.

**Answer: (D) $\tfrac16$**

ukmt-pink-2025-18.title: Spot the squares
ukmt-pink-2025-18.body:
When Patrick has numbered $k^2$ squares, the numbered squares form a $k\times k$ square (for example 1, 4 and 9 squares). Since $2025=45^2$, the figure is a $45\times45$ square. Its side is $45\times0.5=22.5$ cm and its perimeter is $4\times22.5=90$ cm.

**Answer: (B) 90 cm**

ukmt-pink-2025-19.title: Pythagoras in the large circle
ukmt-pink-2025-19.body:
Let the radii of the large and small circles be $R$ and $r$. The centre of the small circle lies on the common diameter line, and the chord is parallel to this line and tangent to the small circle, so the chord is at distance $r$ from that line. The centre of the large circle is on the line, so it is at distance $r$ from the chord. The chord has half-length 8, so $R^2=8^2+r^2$, i.e. $R^2-r^2=64$.

The shaded area is $\pi R^2-\pi r^2=\pi(R^2-r^2)=64\pi\ \text{cm}^2$.

**Answer: (D) $64\pi\ \text{cm}^2$**

ukmt-pink-2025-20.title: Use the divisibility rules in turn
ukmt-pink-2025-20.body:
$abcde$ is a multiple of 5, so $e=5$. The numbers $ab$, $abcd$ and $abcdef$ are even, so $b$, $d$, $f$ are even, taken from $\{2,4,6\}$, and so $a$ and $c$ are 1 and 3 in some order. For $abc$ to be a multiple of 3, $a+b+c=4+b$ must be a multiple of 3, so $b=2$. For $abcd$ to be a multiple of 4, $cd$ must be a multiple of 4; with $c\in\{1,3\}$ and $d\in\{4,6\}$ the multiples of 4 are 16 and 36, so $d=6$. Hence $f=4$. (An example is 123654: $12$, $123$, $1236$, $12365$ and $123654$ all work.)

**Answer: (B) 4**

ukmt-pink-2025-21.title: Sum of the vertices is a multiple of 3

ukmt-pink-2025-24.title: Join IK
ukmt-pink-2025-24.body:
Draw $IK$. Triangle $QIP$ is half of $OQP$, so its area is 30. Triangle $OKP$ has $KP=\tfrac13QP$, so its area is $20$, and $IKP$ is half of $OKP$ ($I$ is the midpoint of $OP$), area $10$. So triangle $QIK$ has area $30-10=20$.

Since $I$ and $K$ are the midpoints of $OP$ and $JP$, $IK\parallel OJ$, so triangles $QLJ$ and $QIK$ are similar, with $QJ:QK=1:2$. Their areas are in the ratio $1:4$, so $\text{area}(QLJ)=\tfrac14\times20=5\ \text{cm}^2$.

**Answer: (B) $5\ \text{cm}^2$**

ukmt-pink-2025-24.title: Equal areas
ukmt-pink-2025-24.body:
Join $LP$ and $LK$. Triangles $QJL$, $JKL$, $KPL$ have equal bases and the same apex $L$, so equal area $x$. Triangles $OLI$ and $LIP$ have equal area $y$ ($I$ is the midpoint of $OP$). Triangle $QIP$ is 30, made of $QJL$, $JKL$, $KPL$ and $LIP$: $3x+y=30$. Triangle $JOP$ is $\tfrac23$ of 60 $=40$, made of $OLI$, $LIP$, $JKL$, $KPL$: $2y+2x=40$. Solving gives $x=5$, $y=15$.

**Answer: (B) $5\ \text{cm}^2$**

ukmt-pink-2025-25.title: Fix the ends and split into cases
ukmt-pink-2025-25.body:
Number the cells of the top row $t_1\dots t_4$ and of the bottom row $b_1\dots b_4$; numbers increase to the right along rows and downwards along columns. So $t_1=1$ and $b_4=8$. The number 2 is next to 1 ($t_2$ or $b_1$) and 7 is next to 8 ($t_4$ or $b_3$).

1. $t_2=2$, $b_3=7$: choose any 2 of 3, 4, 5, 6 for $t_3,t_4$ (in increasing order) and the other two go in $b_1,b_2$ in increasing order: $\binom42=6$ ways.
2. $t_2=2$, $t_4=7$: then 6 must be $b_3$, and $t_3$ can be any of 3, 4, 5, the other two filling $b_1<b_2$: 3 ways.
3. $b_1=2$, $b_3=7$: by symmetry, 3 ways.
4. $b_1=2$, $t_4=7$: then 3 is $t_2$ and 6 is $b_3$, and 4, 5 fill $t_3,b_2$ in either order: 2 ways.

Total $6+3+3+2=14$.

**Answer: (E) 14**
